notes.text: Magnify thee — That is, to gain thee authority among them, as the person whom I have set in Moses's stead, and by whom I will conduct them to the possession of the promised land.

The brink — Hebrew. to the extremity, so far as the river then spread itself, which was now more than ordinary, ver. 15. In Jordan - Within the waters of Jordan, in the first entrance into the river; Where they stood for a season, 'till the river was divided, and then they went into the midst of it, and there abode 'till all the people were passed over. 9. Come hither - To the ark or tabernacle, the place of public assemblies. The Lord your God - Who is now about to give a proof that he is both the Lord, the omnipotent governor of heaven and earth, and all creatures; and your God, in covenant with you, having a tender care and affection for you.

Ye shall know — By experience and sensible evidence. The living God - Not a dull, dead, senseless God, such as the gods of the nations are; but a God of life, and power, and activity to watch over you, and work for you. Among you - Is present with you to strengthen and help you.
Twelve men — For the work described, chap. iv, 2, 3.

The ark of the Lord — That so it may appear this is the Lord's doing, and that in pursuance of his covenant made with Israel. Of all the earth - The Lord of all this globe of earth and water, who therefore can dispose of this river and the adjoining land as he pleaseth. Cut off - The waters which now are united now shall be divided, and part shall flow down the channel towards the dead sea, and the other part that is nearer the spring of the river, and flows down from it, shall stand still. An heap - Being as it were congealed, as the Red-Sea was, Exod. xv, 8, and so kept from overflowing the country.

All the time of harvest — This is meant not of wheat-harvest, but of the barley-harvest, as is manifest from their keeping the passover at their first entrance, chap. v, 10, which was kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, when they were to bring a sheaf of their first-fruits, which were of barley. So that this harvest in those hot countries fell very early in the spring, when rivers used to swell most; partly because of the rains which have fallen all the winter, partly because of the snows which melt and come into the rivers. And this time God chose that the miracle might be more glorious, more amazing and terrible to the Canaanites; and that the Israelites might be entertained at their first entrance with plentiful and comfortable provisions.

Adam — The city Adam being more obscure, is described by its nearness to a more known place, then eminent, but now unknown. The meaning is, that the waters were stopped in their course at that place, and so kept at a distance from the Israelites whilst they passed over. Against Jericho - Here God carried them over, because this part was,

1. The strongest, as having in its neighbourhood an eminent city, a potent king, and a stout and war-like people.

2. The most pleasant and fruitful, and therefore more convenient both for the refreshment of the Israelites after their long and tedious marches, and for their encouragement.

Stood firm — That is, in one and the same place and posture; their feet neither moved by any waters moving in upon them, nor sinking into any mire, which one might think was at the bottom of the river. And this may be opposed to their standing on the bank of the water when they came to it, commanded, ver. 8, which was but for a while, 'till the waters were divided and gone away; and then they were to go farther, even into the midst of Jordan, where they are to stand constantly and fixedly, as this Hebrew word signifies, until all were passed over. The midst of Jordan - In the middle and deepest part of the river. Twelve stones taken up out of the midst of Jordan, and twelve set up there for a memorial, ver. 1-9. The march of the people through Jordan, ver. 10-13. God magnifies Joshua, who commands the priests to come out of Jordan, ver. 14-17. The waters close again, ver. 18, 19. Joshua erects twelve stones for a memorial, ver. 20-24.

glossa.text: *This day will I begin to exalt thee,* etc. ((ID., ubi supra. )) Many wonders were wrought in the wilderness, and nowhere is Jesus said to be exalted. But where the Jordan is passed, it is said to him: *This day will I begin to exalt thee,* etc. For the exaltation of Jesus in the sight of the people takes its beginning from baptism. For they that are baptized are baptized in his death, whose death is accomplished in the exaltation of the cross. Rightly therefore is Jesus then first exalted for each of the faithful, when he comes to the mystery of baptism. Whence: *God exalted him, and gave him the name which is above every name,* etc.
*Of the Lord your God,* etc. ((ADAM., hom. 4 in Jos.)) To the sinner every creature is an enemy, etc., *as far as: who turned the rock into pools of waters, and the stony hill into fountains,* etc.

*The Chanaanite,* possessing, or a possession, or traders, or movable. *The Hethite,* dreading or amazed. *The Hevite,* gathering stones. *The Pherezite,* separating, or scattering abroad. *The Gergesite,* bring near the husbandman, or casting out the husbandman, or a stranger drawing near. *The Amorrhite,* bitter or speaking. *The Jebusite,* treading down, or their manger.

*[The Jordan] had filled the banks at the time of harvest.* The LXX: *As in the days of the wheat harvest.* This seems incredible for our regions, but there (as they relate who have known it) in the beginning of spring is the wheat harvest: and then that river overflows and is filled more than through the winter.

*The waters that came down stood,* etc. ((ADAM., hom. 4.)) I judge that it was not written without a reason of mystery, etc., *as far as* and one Spirit by whom all are purified in baptism, and one God the Father of all.

notes.text: Gathered — Into their own land.
No city — Or rather, no town inhabited, where they might refresh themselves.
The Lord — Hebrew. Unto Jehovah, to the true God. For the Heathens had, many of them, some knowledge of the true God.
Forth — Out of the wilderness.

glossa.text:
*Give praise to the Lord.* ((ID.)) This psalm teaches what we are through ourselves, etc., *as far as* he first admonishes the redeemed to give praise. *Give praise.*

((CASS., AUG.)) Of which there are seven divisions, etc., *as far as* in the seventh he treats of heretics, there, *And they were made few.*
*And from the sea.* ((CASS.)) For the south he puts the sea, understanding thereby the ocean of that quarter; and this can be taken for any quarter of the world whatever.
*They wandered.* ((ID.)) The second part, where is the first temptation, etc., *as far as* fourthly, confession for having been heard, that is, praise.

*Hungry.* ((AUG.)) He signifies the curious of the world, who sought out the truth by divers opinions, and found it not. *Their soul,* etc. God commends himself, because it is expedient for us; we fail that we may ask, and may love him who comes to our aid.

*And he led.* ((AUG.)) As it were, he rescued them from ignorance, showing the way, Christ. Behold, he freed them from error; but in what manner he freed them from the hunger and thirst wherewith they burned, he will say afterwards; but he sets confession first.

notes.text: Holily — In the things of God. Justly - With regard to men. Unblamable - In respect of ourselves. Among you that believe - Who were the constant observers of our behaviour.
By exhorting, we are moved to do a thing willingly; by comforting, to do it joyfully; by charging, to do it carefully.
To his kingdom here, and glory hereafter.

glossa.text: *He called,* with the calling which is according to purpose.

*Therefore.* Because he called you, we give thanks. *He called,* I say, which appears from this, that you quickly and firmly received the word etc. *The hearing of God.* That is, that which we have heard from God, or in which God is heard. *As it is the word of God.* For with so great devotion did they receive the word, that they proved themselves to have understood that it was the doctrine of God.

notes.text: Then — Leaving all converse with his adversaries, whom he now left to the hardness of their hearts.
The scribes sit in the chair of Moses — That is, read and expound the law of Moses, and are their appointed teachers.
All things therefore — Which they read out of the law, and enforce therefrom.
Luke xi, 46.

Their phylacteries — The Jews, understanding those words literally, It shall be as a token upon thy hand, and as frontlets between thine eyes, Exod. xiii, 16. And thou shalt bind these words for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes, Deut. vi, 8; used to wear little scrolls of paper or parchment, bound on their wrist and foreheads, on which several texts of Scripture were writ. These they supposed, as a kind of charm, would preserve them from danger. And hence they seem to have been called phylacteries, or preservatives. The fringes of their garments - Which God had enjoined them to wear, to remind them of doing all the commandments, Num. xv, 38. These, as well as their phylacteries, the Pharisees affected to wear broader and larger than other men. Mark xii, 38. 8, 9, 10. The Jewish rabbis were also called father and master, by their several disciples, whom they required,

1. To believe implicitly what they affirmed, without asking any further reason;

2. To obey implicitly what they enjoined, without seeking further authority. Our Lord, therefore, by forbidding us either to give or receive the title of rabbi, master, or father, forbids us either to receive any such reverence, or to pay any such to any but God.

11. Matt. xx, 26.

12. Whosoever shall exalt himself shall be humbled, and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted - It is observable that no one sentence of our Lord's is so often repeated as this: it occurs, with scarce any variation, at least ten times in the evangelists. Luke xiv, 11; xviii, 14.

glossa.text: *Then he spoke.* Those being refuted who are crafty, he instructs those who are fit, none the less exhorting them to be subject to those men for the sake of the priesthood and the dignity of the name: considering not their works, but their teaching.

*Heavy burdens.* The commandments of the law, with their own traditions mixed in, persuading men to live according to these: and not to come to the easy and delightful grace of Christ; whence above: *Come to me, you that labour and are burdened.*

*But all things.* He said that such teachers are to be heard, not imitated: now he shows the cause for which they cannot believe Christ, that is, because they do all things to be seen of men. For he who desires earthly glory cannot believe Christ preaching heavenly things.
*But you.* For a twofold reason he bids us take heed of them, lest we be led astray by their dissembling, or lest we be inflamed with emulation.

*One is.* Who enlightens man, which no other man does, but only trains him, by teaching he does not bestow understanding. *Your Father.* God is called Father and Master by nature, man by indulgence. Father, that honour may be paid to age, not that he be held the author of life. Master, from fellowship with the true Master, as his messenger: and he is honoured out of reverence for him by whom he is sent.

places.name: The Jordan
places.id: The Jordan River; the crossing point in the Joshua narrative is traditionally placed opposite Jericho near the el-Maghtas ford, modern Qasr el-Yahud.

places.name: Adam
places.id: Tell ed-Damiyeh, on the east bank of the Jordan near the mouth of the Jabbok, c. 25 km north of Jericho. The identification is secure on linguistic and topographic grounds; the site sits at a constriction in the Jordan corridor where landslide damming of the river has been historically attested.

places.name: Zarethan
places.id: An unconfirmed site in the Jordan Valley, named here as the city beside Adam. The leading candidate is Tell es-Saʿidiyeh, c. 28 km north of Jericho on the east bank; Tell Umm Hamad has also been proposed.

places.name: The Dead Sea
places.id: The salt lake at the southern end of the Jordan Rift Valley, c. 80 km long, the lowest point on the earth's surface (−430 m). Called the “Salt Sea” and the “sea of the Arabah” in the Hebrew Bible. Forms the eastern boundary of Judah and the western boundary of Moab.

places.name: Jericho
places.id: Tell es-Sultan, on the western edge of the Jordan Valley c. 10 km NW of the Dead Sea. Excavated by Sellin & Watzinger, Garstang, Kenyon, and most recently by the Italian–Palestinian expedition.

echoes.text: and in the wilderness, where you have seen how that Yahweh your God bore you, as a man does bear his son, in all the way that you went, until you came to this place.”
echoes.note: Paul exhorts 'as a father his own children' (v. 11), echoing 'the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his son (hos ei tis trophophoresei... huion).' Deuteronomy's paternal image of God forming Israel through the wilderness coheres with Paul's claim to have fathered a people and called them to walk worthily (v. 12). Pairs with the maternal-nurse figure of v. 7.

echoes.text: Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.
echoes.note: 'As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him.' Reinforces the fatherly-tenderness simile of v. 11. Faint verbal tie but strongly coherent with the divine-father topos Paul applies to his own pastoral role.

echoes.text: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
echoes.note: 'For whom the Lord loves he reproves, even as a father the son in whom he delights.' Supplies the father-exhorting-son pattern behind Paul's 'exhorting and encouraging' each one as a father (v. 11). Contested, but it belongs to the available paternal-discipline idiom.

echoes.text: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.
echoes.note: God 'calls you into his own kingdom and glory' (v. 12) draws on the OT hope that the saints receive the kingdom; Daniel 7:18 ('the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom') is the seedbed of that eschatological kingdom-and-glory language. Faint and contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Paul charges that they 'killed... their own prophets' (v. 15), the classic Deuteronomistic prophet-killing tradition stated programmatically in Nehemiah's confession: 'they were disobedient... and slew your prophets who testified against them.' High coherence: Paul's polemic is a compressed restatement of this historiographical theme of Israel's persecution of God's messengers.

echoes.text: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: 'They mocked the messengers of God... till the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.' This verse uniquely binds prophet-rejection to the inescapable wrath that 'came upon them to the uttermost' (v. 16), matching both halves of Paul's statement (killing prophets + final wrath). Very strong coherence and volume.

echoes.text: “I have struck your children in vain. They received no correction. Your own sword has devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion.
echoes.note: 'Your own sword has devoured your prophets like a destroying lion.' A concrete instance of the prophet-killing charge that Paul generalizes in v. 15. Recurrence of the motif across the prophets strengthens its presence here.

echoes.text: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]
echoes.note: The narrative of the prophet Uriah, pursued and 'slain with the sword' by the king, is a paradigmatic OT account of killing a prophet who spoke God's word. It supplies historical substance to Paul's 'killed... their own prophets' and the driving-out theme ('drove us out', v. 15).

echoes.text: In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”
echoes.note: 'To fill up their sins always' (v. 16) echoes the measure-of-iniquity motif: 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (anapeplerontai).' The notion that sin must reach a fixed full measure before judgment falls coheres precisely with Paul's logic that wrath comes when sins are 'filled up.'

echoes.text: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.
echoes.note: 'When the transgressors have reached their full measure (pleroumenon ton hamartion), a king... shall arise.' Daniel applies the filling-up-of-sins idea to an eschatological crisis preceding wrath, matching Paul's 'fill up their sins always... wrath has come.' Reinforces Genesis 15:16 within a second-temple judgment framework.

echoes.text: For in the case of the other nations the Sovereign Lord does with longsuffering forbear, until that he punish them when they have attained to the full measure of their sins; but not so judged he as touching us,
echoes.note: Explains that God waits 'until they have reached the full measure of their sins' before punishing — a deuterocanonical articulation of the same measure-of-iniquity theology behind v. 16. Faint as a direct source but confirms the idea's currency in second-temple Judaism (Availability criterion).

echoes.text: The days of visitation have come. The days of reckoning have come. Israel will consider the prophet to be a fool, and the man who is inspired to be insane, because of the abundance of your sins, and because your hostility is great.
echoes.note: 'The days of visitation have come, the days of recompense have come' supplies the prophetic 'the wrath/days have come' formula behind v. 16 ('wrath has come upon them to the uttermost'). Coherent with the prophetic wrath topos; contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: Now will I shortly pour out my wrath on you, and accomplish my anger against you, and will judge you according to your ways; and I will bring on you all your abominations.
echoes.note: 'Now I will shortly pour out my wrath upon you, and accomplish my anger against you.' Ezekiel 7's repeated 'the end has come... wrath' announcement is a candidate background for Paul's compressed 'wrath has come upon them at last.' Faint, contested, but it belongs to the available prophetic-wrath idiom.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The pseudepigraphal phrase 'the wrath of God came upon them to the uttermost (eis telos)' is strikingly close to Paul's wording in v. 16 and is often cited as the nearest verbal parallel. Warranted as a faint, contested second-temple echo illuminating the fixed formula Paul deploys.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.
echoes.note: "They make their phylacteries broad" (v5) directly references tefillin, the binding of the words 'as a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes'; Jesus targets the ostentatious enlargement of this commanded practice.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: "Enlarge the fringes of their garments" (v5) references the commanded tassels (tzitzit) on the corners of garments, given as a reminder of the commandments; the abuse is enlarging them for show.

echoes.text: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.
echoes.note: "A man's pride will bring him low, but the humble in spirit will obtain honor" is the proverbial substrate of v12's exaltation/humiliation reversal.

echoes.text: It shall be for a sign on your hand, and for symbols between your eyes: for by strength of hand Yahweh brought us out of Egypt.”
echoes.note: Parallel phylactery command ('a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes') stands behind the broadened phylacteries of v5.

echoes.text: Don’t exalt yourself in the presence of the king, or claim a place among great men; for it is better that it be said to you, “Come up here,” than that you should be put lower in the presence of the prince, whom your eyes have seen.
echoes.note: "They love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats" (v6) inverts the wisdom counsel not to claim the place of the great but to be invited up; same banqueting-status imagery Jesus uses elsewhere (Luke 14).

echoes.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
echoes.note: "Call no man your father... one is your Father" (v9) echoes 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' — the prophetic insistence on a single divine paternity over the covenant community.

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up.
echoes.note: Hannah's song ('The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and exalts') anticipates the reversal of v12, that the self-exalting are humbled and the humble exalted.

echoes.text: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.
echoes.note: "Exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high" supplies the prophetic reversal formula behind v12.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening.
echoes.note: "Moses' seat" (v2) as the locus of teaching/judging authority evokes Moses sitting to adjudicate for the people; the chair becomes a metaphor for inherited Mosaic teaching office.

echoes.text: You shall do according to the decisions of the verdict which they shall give you from that place which Yahweh chooses. You shall observe to do according to all that they shall teach you: according to the decisions of the law which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the sentence which they shall show you, to the right hand, nor to the left.
echoes.note: The duty to do all that the Levitical judges 'at that place' tell you, not turning aside, underlies Jesus' 'observe and do whatever they tell you' (v3) even while condemning their conduct.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: "You, O LORD, are our Father" supports the one-Father claim of v9 against human honorifics.

echoes.text: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.
echoes.note: "All your children shall be taught by the LORD" undergirds 'one is your teacher' (v8); divine, not rabbinic, instruction is the eschatological norm.

echoes.text: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
echoes.note: "He saves the humble... God saves the lowly" parallels the exalt/humble logic of v12.

echoes.text: The lofty looks of man will be brought low, the haughtiness of men will be bowed down, and Yahweh alone will be exalted in that day. For there will be a day of Yahweh of Armies for all that is proud and haughty, and for all that is lifted up; and it shall be brought low: For all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, for all the oaks of Bashan, For all the high mountains, for all the hills that are lifted up, For every lofty tower, for every […]
echoes.note: The Day of the LORD theme that 'the haughtiness of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone exalted' resonates with v12.

notes.text: That bite — When they are furnished with gifts, and well fed. Prepare war - They do them all the mischief they can.

Night — Heavy calamities. A vision - You shall no more pretend to have a vision, or dare to foretell any thing. And the sun - The hand of God shall be against them, making their sorrows the more dreadful, as darkness by the sun going down at noon.

The seers — So called by the deceived people. Cover their lips - Mourners did thus, Ezek xxiv, 17, 22. So these shall mourn and pine in their shame. No answer - Because the answer they had formerly, pretended to be from God, now appears not to have been from him.
Power — Courage, and vivacity. Of judgment - To discern times and seasons, right from wrong. Might - Resolution.

They — The heads and great ones enlarge, beautify, and fortify, the house in Zion, particularly the temple and the royal palace. Blood - With wealth, which they made themselves masters of by violence, taking away the life of the owners.
Lean — Pretend to trust in him. Among us - As our God and our shield.

For your sake — Because of your sins. The mountain - The mountain, on which the temple stood. This is that passage, which is quoted, Jer. xxvi, 18, which Hezekiah and his princes took well: yea, they repented and so the execution of it did not come in their days. The prosperity of the church, ver. 1-10. Her enemies shall be destroyed, ver. 11-13.
Nation — So he calls the company of his enemies for their great numbers. Man - Probably Achitophel or Absalom.

Send out — That is, actually discover them. Truth - Thy favour, or the light of thy countenance, and the truth of thy promises made to me; or the true-light, the illumination of thy spirit, and the direction of thy gracious providence, whereby I may be led in the right way, to thy holy hill. Hill - Of Zion, the place of God's presence and worship. The church commemorates past mercies, ver. 1-8. Complains of present troubles, ver. 9-16. Professes her integrity, ver. 17-22. Prays for succor, ver. 23-26. To the chief musician for the sons of Korah, Maschil.

glossa.text: *Judge me. ((Ibid.))* He does not ask that his own sins be examined, which is dangerous, but that his cause be made ready apart from the impious, that he may be with the elect: whence he adds: *And distinguish.* The nation that is not holy is the unjust and deceitful man, from whom he is separated in the judgment: but here too lest he be corrupted by them.

*Why do I go sorrowful?* ((AUG.)) He seeks the cause of sadness, which is sin, as justice is the cause of gladness. Isaias on account of sin: *For a little while indeed I made him sorrowful,* for so God punishes.

*Send forth thy light.* ((CASS.)) Because, when he comes, all the sadness of confusion will be taken away. ((AUG.)) Because we now have a sure pledge, since those very things, that is, light and truth, have led the present Church away from her sins, which is the tabernacle.

*And I will go in.* As the high priest to the Holy of holies. ((CASS.)) *And I will go in.* Of the final gladness, for which he gives praise in tribulation, he who above was sad, whence also he strengthens himself.

*I will confess to thee on the harp.* ((AUG.)) He who does the precepts of God, and does not suffer, confesses on the psaltery: but he who does and suffers, which is from the lower nature, *on the harp,* which sounds from below, as the psaltery from above. *On the harp.* ((CASS.)) Behold, he who above was sad about the evils of the world, makes joy for himself out of good understanding. *Why dost thou trouble me? ((Ibid.))* Frequently and vehemently he urges that the sadness of the world must be fled, which extinguishes patience, charity and hope, and confounds the whole life. *The salvation of my countenance.* ((AUG.)) And elsewhere: *Have mercy on me,* etc., *as far as* almsgiving, and prayer which flies to God on those two wings.

notes.text: Holily — In the things of God. Justly - With regard to men. Unblamable - In respect of ourselves. Among you that believe - Who were the constant observers of our behaviour.
By exhorting, we are moved to do a thing willingly; by comforting, to do it joyfully; by charging, to do it carefully.
To his kingdom here, and glory hereafter.

glossa.text: *He called,* with the calling which is according to purpose.

*Therefore.* Because he called you, we give thanks. *He called,* I say, which appears from this, that you quickly and firmly received the word etc. *The hearing of God.* That is, that which we have heard from God, or in which God is heard. *As it is the word of God.* For with so great devotion did they receive the word, that they proved themselves to have understood that it was the doctrine of God.

notes.text: Then — Leaving all converse with his adversaries, whom he now left to the hardness of their hearts.
The scribes sit in the chair of Moses — That is, read and expound the law of Moses, and are their appointed teachers.
All things therefore — Which they read out of the law, and enforce therefrom.
Luke xi, 46.

Their phylacteries — The Jews, understanding those words literally, It shall be as a token upon thy hand, and as frontlets between thine eyes, Exod. xiii, 16. And thou shalt bind these words for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes, Deut. vi, 8; used to wear little scrolls of paper or parchment, bound on their wrist and foreheads, on which several texts of Scripture were writ. These they supposed, as a kind of charm, would preserve them from danger. And hence they seem to have been called phylacteries, or preservatives. The fringes of their garments - Which God had enjoined them to wear, to remind them of doing all the commandments, Num. xv, 38. These, as well as their phylacteries, the Pharisees affected to wear broader and larger than other men. Mark xii, 38. 8, 9, 10. The Jewish rabbis were also called father and master, by their several disciples, whom they required,

1. To believe implicitly what they affirmed, without asking any further reason;

2. To obey implicitly what they enjoined, without seeking further authority. Our Lord, therefore, by forbidding us either to give or receive the title of rabbi, master, or father, forbids us either to receive any such reverence, or to pay any such to any but God.

11. Matt. xx, 26.

12. Whosoever shall exalt himself shall be humbled, and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted - It is observable that no one sentence of our Lord's is so often repeated as this: it occurs, with scarce any variation, at least ten times in the evangelists. Luke xiv, 11; xviii, 14.

glossa.text: *Then he spoke.* Those being refuted who are crafty, he instructs those who are fit, none the less exhorting them to be subject to those men for the sake of the priesthood and the dignity of the name: considering not their works, but their teaching.

*Heavy burdens.* The commandments of the law, with their own traditions mixed in, persuading men to live according to these: and not to come to the easy and delightful grace of Christ; whence above: *Come to me, you that labour and are burdened.*

*But all things.* He said that such teachers are to be heard, not imitated: now he shows the cause for which they cannot believe Christ, that is, because they do all things to be seen of men. For he who desires earthly glory cannot believe Christ preaching heavenly things.
*But you.* For a twofold reason he bids us take heed of them, lest we be led astray by their dissembling, or lest we be inflamed with emulation.

*One is.* Who enlightens man, which no other man does, but only trains him, by teaching he does not bestow understanding. *Your Father.* God is called Father and Master by nature, man by indulgence. Father, that honour may be paid to age, not that he be held the author of life. Master, from fellowship with the true Master, as his messenger: and he is honoured out of reverence for him by whom he is sent.

echoes.text: and in the wilderness, where you have seen how that Yahweh your God bore you, as a man does bear his son, in all the way that you went, until you came to this place.”
echoes.note: Paul exhorts 'as a father his own children' (v. 11), echoing 'the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his son (hos ei tis trophophoresei... huion).' Deuteronomy's paternal image of God forming Israel through the wilderness coheres with Paul's claim to have fathered a people and called them to walk worthily (v. 12). Pairs with the maternal-nurse figure of v. 7.

echoes.text: Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.
echoes.note: 'As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him.' Reinforces the fatherly-tenderness simile of v. 11. Faint verbal tie but strongly coherent with the divine-father topos Paul applies to his own pastoral role.

echoes.text: for whom Yahweh loves, he reproves; even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.
echoes.note: 'For whom the Lord loves he reproves, even as a father the son in whom he delights.' Supplies the father-exhorting-son pattern behind Paul's 'exhorting and encouraging' each one as a father (v. 11). Contested, but it belongs to the available paternal-discipline idiom.

echoes.text: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.
echoes.note: God 'calls you into his own kingdom and glory' (v. 12) draws on the OT hope that the saints receive the kingdom; Daniel 7:18 ('the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom') is the seedbed of that eschatological kingdom-and-glory language. Faint and contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Paul charges that they 'killed... their own prophets' (v. 15), the classic Deuteronomistic prophet-killing tradition stated programmatically in Nehemiah's confession: 'they were disobedient... and slew your prophets who testified against them.' High coherence: Paul's polemic is a compressed restatement of this historiographical theme of Israel's persecution of God's messengers.

echoes.text: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: 'They mocked the messengers of God... till the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.' This verse uniquely binds prophet-rejection to the inescapable wrath that 'came upon them to the uttermost' (v. 16), matching both halves of Paul's statement (killing prophets + final wrath). Very strong coherence and volume.

echoes.text: “I have struck your children in vain. They received no correction. Your own sword has devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion.
echoes.note: 'Your own sword has devoured your prophets like a destroying lion.' A concrete instance of the prophet-killing charge that Paul generalizes in v. 15. Recurrence of the motif across the prophets strengthens its presence here.

echoes.text: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]
echoes.note: The narrative of the prophet Uriah, pursued and 'slain with the sword' by the king, is a paradigmatic OT account of killing a prophet who spoke God's word. It supplies historical substance to Paul's 'killed... their own prophets' and the driving-out theme ('drove us out', v. 15).

echoes.text: In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”
echoes.note: 'To fill up their sins always' (v. 16) echoes the measure-of-iniquity motif: 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (anapeplerontai).' The notion that sin must reach a fixed full measure before judgment falls coheres precisely with Paul's logic that wrath comes when sins are 'filled up.'

echoes.text: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.
echoes.note: 'When the transgressors have reached their full measure (pleroumenon ton hamartion), a king... shall arise.' Daniel applies the filling-up-of-sins idea to an eschatological crisis preceding wrath, matching Paul's 'fill up their sins always... wrath has come.' Reinforces Genesis 15:16 within a second-temple judgment framework.

echoes.text: For in the case of the other nations the Sovereign Lord does with longsuffering forbear, until that he punish them when they have attained to the full measure of their sins; but not so judged he as touching us,
echoes.note: Explains that God waits 'until they have reached the full measure of their sins' before punishing — a deuterocanonical articulation of the same measure-of-iniquity theology behind v. 16. Faint as a direct source but confirms the idea's currency in second-temple Judaism (Availability criterion).

echoes.text: The days of visitation have come. The days of reckoning have come. Israel will consider the prophet to be a fool, and the man who is inspired to be insane, because of the abundance of your sins, and because your hostility is great.
echoes.note: 'The days of visitation have come, the days of recompense have come' supplies the prophetic 'the wrath/days have come' formula behind v. 16 ('wrath has come upon them to the uttermost'). Coherent with the prophetic wrath topos; contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: Now will I shortly pour out my wrath on you, and accomplish my anger against you, and will judge you according to your ways; and I will bring on you all your abominations.
echoes.note: 'Now I will shortly pour out my wrath upon you, and accomplish my anger against you.' Ezekiel 7's repeated 'the end has come... wrath' announcement is a candidate background for Paul's compressed 'wrath has come upon them at last.' Faint, contested, but it belongs to the available prophetic-wrath idiom.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The pseudepigraphal phrase 'the wrath of God came upon them to the uttermost (eis telos)' is strikingly close to Paul's wording in v. 16 and is often cited as the nearest verbal parallel. Warranted as a faint, contested second-temple echo illuminating the fixed formula Paul deploys.

echoes.text: You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.
echoes.note: "They make their phylacteries broad" (v5) directly references tefillin, the binding of the words 'as a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes'; Jesus targets the ostentatious enlargement of this commanded practice.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: "Enlarge the fringes of their garments" (v5) references the commanded tassels (tzitzit) on the corners of garments, given as a reminder of the commandments; the abuse is enlarging them for show.

echoes.text: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.
echoes.note: "A man's pride will bring him low, but the humble in spirit will obtain honor" is the proverbial substrate of v12's exaltation/humiliation reversal.

echoes.text: It shall be for a sign on your hand, and for symbols between your eyes: for by strength of hand Yahweh brought us out of Egypt.”
echoes.note: Parallel phylactery command ('a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes') stands behind the broadened phylacteries of v5.

echoes.text: Don’t exalt yourself in the presence of the king, or claim a place among great men; for it is better that it be said to you, “Come up here,” than that you should be put lower in the presence of the prince, whom your eyes have seen.
echoes.note: "They love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats" (v6) inverts the wisdom counsel not to claim the place of the great but to be invited up; same banqueting-status imagery Jesus uses elsewhere (Luke 14).

echoes.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
echoes.note: "Call no man your father... one is your Father" (v9) echoes 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' — the prophetic insistence on a single divine paternity over the covenant community.

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up.
echoes.note: Hannah's song ('The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and exalts') anticipates the reversal of v12, that the self-exalting are humbled and the humble exalted.

echoes.text: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.
echoes.note: "Exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high" supplies the prophetic reversal formula behind v12.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening.
echoes.note: "Moses' seat" (v2) as the locus of teaching/judging authority evokes Moses sitting to adjudicate for the people; the chair becomes a metaphor for inherited Mosaic teaching office.

echoes.text: You shall do according to the decisions of the verdict which they shall give you from that place which Yahweh chooses. You shall observe to do according to all that they shall teach you: according to the decisions of the law which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the sentence which they shall show you, to the right hand, nor to the left.
echoes.note: The duty to do all that the Levitical judges 'at that place' tell you, not turning aside, underlies Jesus' 'observe and do whatever they tell you' (v3) even while condemning their conduct.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: "You, O LORD, are our Father" supports the one-Father claim of v9 against human honorifics.

echoes.text: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.
echoes.note: "All your children shall be taught by the LORD" undergirds 'one is your teacher' (v8); divine, not rabbinic, instruction is the eschatological norm.

echoes.text: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
echoes.note: "He saves the humble... God saves the lowly" parallels the exalt/humble logic of v12.

echoes.text: The lofty looks of man will be brought low, the haughtiness of men will be bowed down, and Yahweh alone will be exalted in that day. For there will be a day of Yahweh of Armies for all that is proud and haughty, and for all that is lifted up; and it shall be brought low: For all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, for all the oaks of Bashan, For all the high mountains, for all the hills that are lifted up, For every lofty tower, for every […]
echoes.note: The Day of the LORD theme that 'the haughtiness of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone exalted' resonates with v12.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Send out your light and your truth; let them lead us.
Bring us to your holy hill, to the place where you dwell.
The greatest among you will be your servant.
All who humble themselves will be lifted up.
We have followed false lights and louder voices.
Lead us, O God, to your altar and our joy.
Come, let us worship the God who lifts the lowly.
We come, servants of the Servant. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: When the way is dark and the false guides cry peace where there is no peace, one prayer steadies us: send out your light.
Send out your light and your truth, O God.
Let that light go before us like a lamp on the road, leading up to the holy hill, to the altar, to the joy of God.
Send out your light and your truth, O God.
There we learn the only greatness Christ will bless: the towel, the basin, the servant's place.
Send out your light and your truth, O God.
For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and all who humble themselves will be raised.
Send out your light and your truth, O God.
So come out of the shadows into the light, and worship.
Send out your light and your truth, O God. Amen.
